items.title: Elsevier Launches AI Assistant for Healthcare E-books
items.excerpt: Elsevier's Nora AI lets healthcare students ask questions about their course materials and get answers without leaving the e-book. The assistant is scoped to the publisher's own licensed content rather than the open web.
items.why: A major educational publisher shipping an in-book AI assistant turns the e-book from a container into an interface — a concrete brief for anyone designing reading products.

items.title: Google’s AI note-taking app now allows you to interact with books
items.excerpt: Gemini Notebook's new “Expert Intelligence” feature lets users pull licensed Play Books titles in as sources and question them directly, putting published books inside an AI research workspace.
items.why: Books becoming a first-class AI source type changes discovery, licensing and how publishers think about a title's digital surface.

items.title: E-Books: Google Announces Launch of “Expert Intelligence” Feature For Gemini Notebook
items.excerpt: Library-side write-up of Google's Expert Intelligence launch, detailing which publisher content is licensed into Gemini Notebook and how citations back to the source book are handled.
items.why: The librarian framing surfaces the licensing and citation mechanics that publishers and reading-product designers actually have to negotiate.

items.title: “A Secure Environment to Explore”: The AI Sandbox Initiative For Staff at the Library of Congress
items.excerpt: The Library of Congress has stood up an internal AI sandbox so staff can test generative tools against collections work in a controlled environment before anything touches public services.
items.why: A rare, concrete model for how a collections institution rolls out AI to practitioners — sandbox first, workflow second — that any content org can copy.

items.title: Read These Books Before You Enter the AI and Social Media Debates
items.excerpt: A curated nonfiction reading list mapping the current arguments about generative AI and platform culture, aimed at readers who want the primary texts rather than the discourse.
items.why: Useful as the reading-side counterpart to tool news — what a creative professional should actually read to argue about AI competently.

items.title: We Can Now Track AI-generated Content. It Doesn’t Solve the Real Problem.
items.excerpt: With watermarking and provenance tooling now shipping, the piece argues detection alone answers the wrong question: publishing still has to decide what level of AI assistance is acceptable and disclose it.
items.why: Moves the conversation from “can we detect it” to “what is the editorial policy” — the question every publishing and design team is dodging.

items.title: Recognizing ‘Human’ Contributions, Longlist Revealed for the 26th getAbstract International Book Award
items.excerpt: The 2026 getAbstract award longlist is explicitly framed around recognizing human authorship and contribution, with winners to be announced October 8 at the Frankfurt Book Fair.
items.why: Prizes are starting to define “human-made” as a category — an early signal of how authorship credit gets certified in an AI-saturated market.

items.title: Are Amazon and Other AI Companies Destroying Books to Train AI?
items.excerpt: ALLi's news summary on reports that AI firms are buying physical books, cutting the spines off and scanning them for training corpora — and what that means for authors' licensing leverage.
items.why: Indie-author framing of the training-data supply chain, with the practical question of whether authors can license instead of being scanned.

items.title: AI Companies are buying hardcover books and destroying them
items.excerpt: Report on AI companies acquiring print runs of hardcovers purely to destructively scan them, sidestepping licensing negotiations with publishers entirely.
items.why: The physical-to-corpus pipeline made literal — a vivid, concrete story about where model training data for text actually comes from.

items.title: Calibre ebook manager lets you generate AI book covers in a click
items.excerpt: Calibre 9.14 adds generative AI cover creation to the open-source e-book manager, letting users produce and swap in a cover image from a prompt inside the library tool itself.
items.why: Cover generation arriving as a default feature in mainstream reader software — a direct hit on book-cover design work and on what readers now expect a jacket to be.

items.title: AI vs. Human Audiobook Narration: A Blinded Survey of 1,000 Listeners
items.excerpt: A blinded listening study of 1,000 audiobook consumers testing whether people can tell AI narration from human narration — and whether knowing changes how much they say they'd pay.
items.why: Actual listener data instead of vibes on synthetic narration — the number publishers and narrators will both cite in the next contract fight.

items.title: Amazon Rips Up Rare Books to Train AI (Self-Publishing News Podcast)
items.excerpt: Dan Holloway's weekly news round-up covering Amazon shredding rare books for AI training, Kobo's return to Best Buy, and Ingram's new Covered platform for indie authors.
items.why: Fast weekly briefing that bundles the AI training story with the retail and tooling moves indie authors have to react to.

items.title: Anthropic Adds Watermarks to Claude’s AI-Generated Text
items.excerpt: Anthropic is watermarking text generated by Claude, raising new questions about AI transparency, provenance and disclosure for AI-assisted books.
items.why: Provenance marks moving into the writing stack directly affects how authors and publishers will have to declare AI assistance.

items.title: Podcast: Amazon Kindle and AI Destruction of books
items.excerpt: Good e-Reader's podcast unpacks the destructive scanning of hardcovers for AI corpora alongside Kindle pricing and hardware changes affecting readers.
items.why: Reader-device context for the training-data story — how the same shift lands on the consumer end of the reading stack.
